title: Bag With Instant Random Pick
statement:
Build a bag of integers. Unlike a set, a bag can hold several copies of the same value. Support these operations, each in O(1) average time:

  • insert(val) adds one copy of val. Returns true if the bag held no copy of val before, false otherwise. The copy is added either way.
  • remove(val) removes one copy of val if there is one. Returns true if a copy was removed, false if there was none.
  • getRandom() returns a random element of the bag, where every copy is equally likely. A value with 3 copies in a bag of 4 elements comes back with probability 3/4. It is only called on a non-empty bag.

Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first one creates the empty bag. Because getRandom is random, the checker accepts any value in the bag at that moment. On long runs of getRandom it also checks that every value shows up and that each value appears roughly in proportion to its number of copies.

examples.out: [null, true, false, true, true, 6, true, false]
examples.why: The second 6 is added but returns false because a 6 was already there. Removing 6 takes away one copy, so the bag is {6, 2} and getRandom may return 6 or 2. Two removals empty out the 6s, so a third fails.
The bag is {1, 1, 4}: getRandom returns 1 with probability 2/3 and 4 with probability 1/3. Picking a distinct value uniformly would be wrong.

constraints: getRandom is only called on a non-empty bag
hints: Start from the set version: an array of values for random access, plus a map from value to its slot. What breaks when a value can sit in several slots?
Map each value to the set of all array positions holding a copy. getRandom stays a random index into the array, which automatically weights values by their copy count.
To remove one copy, take any position i of that value, move the array's last element into slot i, update the moved value's position set (add i, drop the old last index), and pop the array.

explain.intuition:
The weighting comes for free if every copy has its own slot in an array: a uniform random index then lands on a value with 3 copies three times as often as on a value with one. The hard part is removing one copy in O(1). Deleting from the middle of an array shifts everything after it.

The fix is the same swap trick as for the plain set: move the last element into the hole and shrink the array by one. To find a hole quickly, keep a map from each value to the set of positions where its copies sit. When the last element moves, its position set must swap its old index for the new one. Do that update in the right order, adding the new index before removing the old one, because when you remove the last slot itself, both are the same index.
steps: Keep vals, an array with one slot per copy, and pos, a map from value to a set of indexes in vals.
insert(val): note whether pos[val] was empty, push val, add its index to pos[val], and return that note.
remove(val): if pos[val] is empty, return false. Otherwise take any index i from it.
Move last = vals[end] into slot i, add i to pos[last], delete end from pos[last], pop vals, and return true.
pitfalls: Picking a random distinct value instead of a random copy. In a bag of {1, 1, 4}, 1 must come back two thirds of the time.
Removing the old index from the moved value's set before adding the new one. When i is the last slot, you end up with a stale index pointing past the end.
Storing only one position per value. With duplicates, removing one copy would lose track of the others.

solutions.title: Plain array, search to remove
solutions.idea: Keep every copy in an array. getRandom is a random index; remove finds a copy by scanning and splices it out.

solutions.title: Array of copies + value → set of positions
solutions.idea: Each copy has a slot, so a random index weights values by count. Removal fills the hole with the last slot and fixes that value's position set.
solutions.py:
import random


class RandomizedCollection:
    def __init__(self):
        self.vals = []
        self.pos = defaultdict(set)

    def insert(self, val: int) -> bool:
        fresh = not self.pos[val]
        self.pos[val].add(len(self.vals))
        self.vals.append(val)
        return fresh

    def remove(self, val: int) -> bool:
        if not self.pos[val]:
            return False
        i = self.pos[val].pop()
        end = len(self.vals) - 1
        last = self.vals[end]
        self.vals[i] = last
        self.pos[last].add(i)  # add first: when i == end these cancel out correctly
        self.pos[last].discard(end)
        self.vals.pop()
        return True

    def getRandom(self) -> int:
        return self.vals[random.randrange(len(self.vals))]
